title: James McAvoy Calls “Split” the Only Film That Consistently Pays Him, Says Variety
body:
James McAvoy has revealed that the 2016 psychological thriller Split, directed by M. Night Shyamalan, remains the only movie in his extensive résumé that still generates regular residual checks. The Scottish actor, whose career spans high‑profile dramas, blockbuster franchises and indie thrillers, disclosed the surprising detail during a recent interview, underscoring how the film’s enduring popularity continues to pay dividends long after its theatrical run.

McAvoy’s comment highlights a broader industry reality: residuals—payments made to actors when a film is rebroadcast, streamed, or otherwise re‑exhibited—can be unpredictable and often taper off quickly. While many of his past projects, such as the critically acclaimed Atonement (2007) and the commercially successful X‑Men: First Class (2011), enjoyed strong box‑office returns, the long‑term revenue streams from those titles have largely dried up for the actor. By contrast, Split has maintained a steady flow of viewership across multiple platforms, translating into consistent earnings for McAvoy.

The film’s staying power can be attributed to several factors. First, Shyamalan’s reputation for crafting twist‑laden narratives has cultivated a dedicated fan base that revisits his work repeatedly. Split introduced audiences to the unsettling character of Kevin Wendell Crumb, a man with 23 distinct personalities, a premise that continues to spark discussion on social media and in fan forums. Second, the movie’s distribution strategy—initially a theatrical release followed by swift availability on streaming services—ensured that it remained accessible to a wide audience long after its opening weekend. Platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and later Disney+ have kept the title in rotation, generating ongoing royalty payments for its cast.

McAvoy’s filmography illustrates the uneven nature of residual income in Hollywood. After his breakout role in The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, he built a diverse portfolio that includes the haunting Speak No Evil (2022), the period drama Atonement, and the superhero ensemble X‑Men: First Class. Yet, the contractual terms of each project differ markedly. Some agreements, particularly for large studio productions, involve a front‑loaded salary with limited backend participation, while independent or mid‑budget films like Split often include profit‑share clauses that can become lucrative if the title enjoys a long tail on digital platforms. McAvoy’s experience underscores how strategic negotiations and the nature of a film’s distribution can dramatically affect an actor’s long‑term earnings.

Industry analysts note that the shift toward streaming has reshaped residual calculations. Unlike the traditional television syndication model, where shows earned predictable per‑episode fees, streaming services negotiate bespoke deals that factor in view counts, subscriber impact and global reach. For actors, this can mean larger, albeit less transparent, payouts for titles that become “evergreen” content. McAvoy’s situation exemplifies how a film that might have seemed modest in its initial box‑office performance can evolve into a steady revenue source when it finds a permanent home in the streaming ecosystem.

Looking ahead, McAvoy’s revelation may prompt other performers to scrutinize the residual structures of their contracts, especially as the industry continues to pivot toward digital distribution. As streaming platforms expand their libraries and invest in long‑term licensing, the potential for older titles to generate recurring income grows. For McAvoy, Split serves as a reminder that a single, well‑placed role can provide financial stability long after the cameras stop rolling, and it may influence how he, and his peers, approach future projects in an ever‑changing entertainment landscape.
